_comment: THE cross-language log timestamp contract. Go, TypeScript and elisp each
assert their own renderer against this file, which is the only mechanism
that makes a divergence between the three fail loudly instead of quietly.
Within a language the renderer is genuinely shared: Go has one module
(agent-shim/logging, imported by the daemon, the store and the sidecar),
TypeScript has one source (agent-shim/logging/ts/timestamp.ts, imported by
the shim and the webapp), and elisp has one defconst in core.el. Three
runtimes in three languages cannot compile one source, so this file is the
seam where the three are held to the same answer.
It pins the REPRESENTATION, not the clock. Every record still stamps the
instant its own runtime observed; what may never differ is how that
instant is written down, because a daemon record and a webapp record that
read as different clocks cannot be interleaved by a human or sorted by a
tool.
LOCAL TIME IS DELIBERATE. An operator reading these logs is reading them
on the machine that wrote them, and correlating a log line against what
they just watched happen in the editor is the dominant use. UTC forced
that reader to do zone arithmetic on every line to answer 'is this the
event I just saw?'.
SIX FRACTIONAL DIGITS ARE DELIBERATE, AND FIXED-WIDTH. Go's RFC3339Nano
drops trailing zeros, so a record landing on a whole second rendered
shorter than its neighbors and the two no longer sorted lexically against
each other. JavaScript resolves instants only to milliseconds and pads the
remaining three digits with zeros rather than emitting a narrower field.
One instant, written the way this contract requires. The rendering is
the one a machine whose local zone is UTC produces, which is the only
rendering that is the same on every developer's machine.
